This is a concrete blocker for me, not just an edge case.

The session’s stored working directory can become stale when the original directory is deleted, renamed, moved, or—as in my case—was a temporary directory created by the host application and no longer exists.

Once `session.directory` points to a non-existing path, I can no longer resume or fork that session, even if I explicitly provide a valid directory:

`opencode run --session <session-id> --fork --dir <existing-directory>`

OpenCode still tries to resolve the stale stored directory and fails before the requested `--dir` can take effect.

I verified that the session itself is otherwise intact: changing only its `directory` field in `opencode.db` to a valid path makes the same session resume successfully with its full history.

So there is currently no supported recovery path for this situation. The session is effectively blocked unless the database is edited manually.

An explicit `--dir` should either override the stale stored directory for the fork/resume, or OpenCode should provide another supported way to rebind the session to a valid directory.

Another instance of this, with a different shape: a 2.0.9 install was **downgraded to 2.0.8** because the update service's answer for `current=2.0.9` moved backwards.

## Environment

- opencode version: 2.0.9 → 2.0.8 (installed automatically at 2026-09-19 09:21:29 UTC)
- OS: Windows 11 (Windows_NT 10.0.26200, win32 x64)
- Install/channel: bun global install (`~/.bun/bin`), channel `latest`, `local=false`
- Active plugins: none at the time (a plugin was installed later that day)

## Evidence

CLI log (`~/.local/share/opencode/log/opencode.log`, UTC):

```
09:21:10 level=INFO message="update check" current=2.0.9 latest=2.0.8
09:21:10 level=INFO message="OpenCode update available" current=2.0.9 latest=2.0.8 action=notify
09:21:24 level=INFO message="spawning process" command=bun args="[... \"install\",\"--global\",\"--trust\",\"--cache-dir\",\"C:\\Users\\<user>\\.cache\\opencode\\update-268SSX\",\"@opencode/cli@2.0.8\"]"
09:21:29 level=INFO message="updated OpenCode" from=2.0.9 to=2.0.8 method=bun
```

Earlier the same day the same check reported `current=2.0.9 latest=2.0.9` (`action=up-to-date`, 08:54:53 UTC), so the service's "latest" for `latest/cli/npm` changed from 2.0.9 to 2.0.8 between 08:54 and 09:21 UTC.

The update API still answers this way (checked 2026-09-19 ~09:35 UTC):

```
$ curl -s "https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/cli/npm?current=2.0.9"
{"channel":"latest","name":"cli","distribution":"npm","version":"2.0.8","metadata":{"package":"@opencode/cli","github":{"sha":"0a611129...","run_id":"35325251492","run_attempt":"1","actor":"Hona","ref":"refs/heads/v2"}},"active":false,"minimum":false,"time_created":1789722595958,"time_updated":1789722595958}
```

Meanwhile `@opencode/cli@2.0.9` is published on npm (dist-tag `latest`, published 2026-09-19T05:11:15Z) and `v2.0.9` is tagged in the repo. So any client on 2.0.9 is currently told that 2.0.8 is "available".

## Expected

The update prompt/install should only fire when `latest > current` (semver-greater), so a client that is ahead of the update service can never be downgraded.

## Actual

2.0.9 was downgraded to 2.0.8; OpenCode even logged it as `updated OpenCode from=2.0.9 to=2.0.8`. (Same missing semver-gt guard noted in #49660.)

Same enforcement now blocks **Muse Spark 1.3** (Meta's model served via OpenCode's own gateways: `opencode/muse-spark-1.3*` on Zen/Console and `opencode-go/muse-spark-1.3*` on Console Go). Every request fails, even a plain "hi" in a fresh chat, with:

```
[invalid_request_error] JSON schema exceeds the maximum nesting depth of 10 levels
```

Reproduction data (2026-09-19, current stable, Windows):

1. **Bare config (zero MCPs) + Muse Spark 1.3 → works** — OpenCode's built-in tool schemas are within the cap.
2. **Vercel MCP (`https://mcp.vercel.com`, 212 tools) + Muse Spark 1.3 → fails on every message** — the check is per-request, so one deep tool disables all tool use.
3. Measured tool schema depth directly against `mcp.vercel.com` using the MCP SDK: **12 tools nest 10–15 levels deep** — `create_flag` (15), `update_flag` (14), `update_flag_segment` (13), `create_sandboxes_v2/v3/v4` + `update_sandbox` (12), `put_firewall_config` / `update_project` / `update_session_network_policy` (11), `create_connector` / `update_firewall_config` (10).
4. **Workaround confirmed working:** a wholly-disabling `permission` deny (e.g. `"vercel_create_flag": "deny"` in `opencode.json`) removes the tool registration entirely so its schema is never sent (`ToolRegistry.materialize`), after which Muse Spark 1.3 works with the remaining 200 vercel tools (verified incl. a live read call from the model).

Request: could OpenCode flatten/depth-cap tool schemas per provider at request time (or expose a per-tool exclusion for depth-capped models)? That would restore the withheld tools without user-side config. Happy to share more measurements if useful.

That rules out both of my guesses, which is useful — it means the ruleset reaching the check at execution time is not the one `debug agent` prints.

Walking the path on `dev` with those two facts in hand:

- `evaluateInput` gets its rules from `configured(sessionID, agent)`, which is `agents.resolve(agentID ?? session.agent)` then `agent?.permissions ?? missingAgentPermissions`.
- `missingAgentPermissions` is `[{ action: "*", resource: "*", effect: "deny" }]` — an unresolvable agent fails **closed**, so a missing agent can't produce this.
- The V1 → V2 migration of `permission.bash` (`v1/config/migrate.ts`) has no platform branch; it just maps entries to rules.
- `bash.ts` calls `permission.assert` unconditionally with `resources: [input.command]`, so the evaluation isn't gated on anything.

Since an explicit `"echo *": "deny"` also fails, `Wildcard.match` is out too — that leaves `agents.resolve()` returning an agent whose `.permissions` is populated differently at runtime than what `debug agent` reads. `debug agent` reads the config; `configured()` goes through the **session's** stored agent.

Two things would separate those, if you're able:

1. Does the same deny work on Windows for a **primary** agent — same rule, no subagent involved? If the primary is denied and only the subagent isn't, it's rule propagation into the spawned agent rather than config loading.
2. Does a **top-level** `permission.bash` (outside any agent block) deny on Windows? That path doesn't depend on agent resolution at all.

If the primary agent is also allowed through, it's config-to-session; if only the subagent is, it's the subagent spawn. Worth noting #49367 and #49342 also describe subagent-scoped behaviour diverging from the parent, so there may be a shared cause.

I'd like to work on this one. Traced it down: the autoselecting resource in packages/app/src/pages/layout.tsx auto-navigates on load using server.projects.last(), which is a browser localStorage value keyed only by server host:port, not by launch directory. Since opencode web reuses the same default port across separate invocations, a stale "last project" for that port gets reused even when launched from a different project.  It is self-reinforcing since navigating persists it as the new "last". Planning to make the autoselect prefer the server's actual current launch directory over the stale last value when one exists. 
Will open a PR referencing this issue.
